newsitem.title: USA: New FTC rules seen having little impact on mergers.
newsitem.headline: New FTC rules seen having little impact on mergers.

text.p: New U.S. regulations aimed at speeding up merger cases are expected to have little impact on most transactions, which typically receive swift indications about whether they will be fraught with antitrust problems.

Only a small percentage of mergers would likely be affected by the new rules unveiled on Wednesday by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), according to merger experts and attorneys. The regulations cover transactions in which the commission already has filed an injunction to block the deal. But most cases with antitrust implications never get to that point.
In most cases, "two parties are more likely to walk away than to risk an antitrust problem," said one investment banker who did not want to be identified.

For example, Rite Aid Corp withdrew its friendly $1.8 billion bid for rival Revco D.S. Inc in April after the FTC and state regulators vowed to go to court to block the deal. They contended a merger of the nation's two largest drugstore chains would drive up consumer prices.
Last year, Microsoft Corp dropped its $2 billion acquisition of Intuit Inc after the Justice Deparment filed suit to block the deal on antitrust grounds.
Most merger experts could not immediately name a pending merger case that would be affected by the new rules, which are being unveiled in a record year for corporate transactions.

Under the new regulations, an FTC administrative judge must reach a decision within a year after the commission files a complaint in antitrust cases. Also, companies facing a government lawsuit could seek to place the case on a "fast track" for resolution by the commission within 13 months.
"There have never been very strict timetables before. As a responsible agency, they are responding to a valid public concern," said John Collins, attorney at Dewey Ballantine.
But 13 months can still be a long time to wait.
"In the life of a company that is in the throes of strategic change, a year is an eternity," the banker said.
